title: FedPAT: Federated Test-Time Adaptation via Prototype Affinity Topology
one_liner: When a federated model sees new data from a new client, it stabilizes predictions by trusting the structural relationships between class prototypes, not the local feature measurements.
lead: Federated learning lets many devices train one model together while keeping their data private. But when each device has different kinds of data, or when the world shifts — the camera angle changes, the lighting shifts, the weather worsens — the local measurements of feature patterns become unreliable. FedPAT discovers that even though each device measures features very differently, the neighborhood structure around each class stays the same: "cat is close to dog, far from car". By remembering these stable relationships globally and then checking new data against them, FedPAT makes predictions honest even when the local patterns go haywire.

paras: Imagine a fleet of delivery robots across different cities. Each robot has a camera that must recognize objects. They train together to save bandwidth and protect privacy — a method called federated learning. But each city has different lighting, seasons, and weather. When a robot trained in sunlight suddenly works at night, its measurements of how "bright" or "red" an image region is become useless.

A naive fix is to have each robot adapt on its own using new unlabeled images from its current location. But adaptation based on local measurements — averaging the features of all cats the robot sees today — is fragile. If today's cats are all photographed from above, the average cat-feature becomes "cat from above", and tomorrow's side-view cat looks alien and gets misclassified.

callout.html: Local feature statistics (the average brightness or shape of a cat-image) change wildly under distribution shift, but what stays the same is which classes are neighbors: cats remain close to dogs and far from cars, even under massive lighting changes.

panels.title: 1. Normal federated learning
panels.caption: Many devices train one shared model privately.

panels.title: 2. But the world shifts
panels.caption: Local feature patterns collapse: what was hot (cat) becomes free (cold/dark).

panels.title: 3. But class relationships hold firm
panels.viz_args: Cat stays near Dog; both stay far from Car
panels.caption: The neighborhood of each class barely shifts, even when lighting fails.

panels.title: 4. FedPAT learns the neighborhoods
panels.caption: A global topology (neighborhood map) is stored and passed to all devices.

panels.title: 5. New device uses the neighborhoods
panels.caption: When the new device sees an image, it checks: does it fit in the known neighborhoods?

steps.text: During training on the source devices, FedPAT computes a prototype (an archetypal example) for each class and measures which prototypes sit near each other.
Each device sends its prototype neighborhood map to the central server; the server averages them into one stable global neighborhood structure called the prototype affinity topology.
When a new device arrives with new data, it receives the global topology as a structural prior — a belief about which classes should be neighbors.
For each incoming image, the device computes local features and diffuses these features along the known topology, spreading information through the neighborhood to stabilize each class score.
The device blends the topology-diffused scores with its own feature-based scores and does a lightweight optimization step, producing a stable prediction.

paras: Instead of trusting local feature statistics for test-time adaptation — the mean feature of all cats seen so far — FedPAT changes the reference frame: it leans on the structural relationships (neighborhoods) between class prototypes. This topology remains stable across distribution shifts because it measures which classes *should* be similar, not the absolute feature values.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: Prototype Affinity Topology
hidden.name: prototype affinity topology
paras: The prototype affinity topology (PAT) is a map of distances between class prototypes. For each class (cat, dog, car), the model learns one representative example (the prototype). PAT then measures: how far is cat-prototype from dog-prototype? How far is cat-prototype from car-prototype? This forms a distance matrix — a table that says "on a scale of 0 to 1, how close is each class to every other class?"

FedPAT estimates PAT by computing prototypes from training data on each source device, then averaging all these prototype-distance-tables together at the server. This averages out the noise from local distribution shifts and keeps the stable relationships. When a new device arrives, it receives this global PAT and uses it to check whether new images fit the expected neighborhood structure.

heat.caption: Darker cells are stronger relationships (Cat and Dog are close; both far from Car). Highlights show the global PAT and its stability across clients.

reads.html: The prototype affinity topology is just a memory of which classes belong near each other. It stays true even when cameras, lighting, or seasons change, because it was built by averaging what many devices saw.

The prototype affinity topology is computed as the covariance or distance structure among class prototypes, aggregated across source clients via federated averaging, and constrains (steers) test-time adaptation to stay coherent with the learned neighborhood structure.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: Stable structure survives chaos
paras: Feature values (the exact numbers in a feature vector, which is just a list of measurements about the image) are fragile under distribution shift, but the relationships among prototypes are much more stable. When the prototype affinity topology says "cat-prototype sits close to dog-prototype in feature space", that relationship persists even when the lighting darkens or the camera angle shifts.

Here is the causal chain: First, FedPAT learns PAT by averaging prototype neighborhoods from many source devices, so PAT captures consensus relationships that noise and local drift have already cancelled out. Second, when a new device receives PAT, it has a structural belief: "if this image looks like a cat, then other nearby classes should also have high scores; if it looks like a car, then cat and dog should have lower scores." Third, the device uses diffusion — spreading belief through the neighborhood like water spreading through connected pipes — to adjust raw scores based on whether they fit the known topology. A score that violates the topology gets dampened. This forces coherence and filters out wild local-shift noise.

The lightweight optimization step at the end refines predictions by moving the feature representation a tiny amount to better fit both the local image and the global topology constraint. This is the safety net: even if the topology is wrong, the device can adjust slightly without overtraining.

stages.s: New unlabeled image from unseen device
Extract raw feature vector and compute initial class scores
Use global PAT to adjust scores via diffusion through class neighborhoods
Blend topology-adjusted scores with original feature-based scores
Lightweight optimization: nudge feature slightly to fit topology constraint
Final prediction that respects both the image and the global structure

math.words: loss is local feature mismatch plus a penalty for violating the prototype topology plus a light regularization to prevent over-adaptation
math.equation: L_test = L_feature(f, y) + lambda * L_topology(f, PAT) + mu * ||f - f_init||^2
symbols: how far off the current feature f is from what the image y should be
the feature vector for this image
penalty for how badly the current features violate the learned prototype neighborhoods
the global prototype affinity topology (neighborhood distance matrix)
how much to trust the topology versus the local signal
how much to prevent drifting far from the starting features

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose we see an image that looks partially like a cat. Local features give it cat-score 0.5 and dog-score 0.1 (very different, violates PAT).
PAT says cat and dog should both be high or both be low (they are neighbors in the topology).
L_topology sees this violation and computes penalty = 0.3 (big disagreement with topology).
L_feature computes mismatch = 0.2 (the image is somewhat ambiguous).
During optimization, the model nudges dog-score from 0.1 upward toward 0.4, shrinking L_topology to 0.1. New loss = 0.2 + 0.08 + 0.05 = 0.33.
The topology constraint pulled dog-score up because PAT knows cat and dog are neighbors; the model now predicts ambiguous-but-coherent instead of certain-but-topologically-wrong.

math.note: This equation forces the model to balance fitting the image (via local features) against fitting the global structure (the topology), while staying close to the original trained features.

charts.title: Naive federated learning (no adaptation)
charts.note: Local feature statistics fail under shift; the model collapses on new data but also forgets how to handle old data.

charts.title: FedPAT (topology-guided adaptation)
charts.note: Topology provides a stable anchor. The model adapts to the shift while retaining memory of source patterns because the reference frame (neighborhood structure) stays true across shifts.

items.b: Topology learned on biased source devices.
items.html: If the source clients all happen to be biased in the same direction (e.g. all mostly daytime cameras), the global PAT will bake in that bias. A new device with very different data (night cameras) will find that the stored topology does not apply well. The diffusion step will then pull it toward the wrong neighborhoods.

items.b: Mismatch between class count and topology.
items.html: If a new unseen device has classes that were not in the source clients' training, there is no prototype for them, and PAT cannot guide adaptation. The topology is silent on how the new class relates to the old ones.

If the topology spreads belief too aggressively (lambda is too high), the model will blur class distinctions. All classes start looking equally plausible because every class pulls on every other via the topology.

FedPAT works best when source clients are diverse enough that their averaged PAT is a genuine consensus, not a majority illusion. The hyperparameters lambda and mu must be tuned to the magnitude of shift expected; if shifts are mild, lambda should be lower (trust local features more).

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small federated learning setup with 3 source clients (each with a different subset of CIFAR-10, the standard small-image test set) and simulate a distribution shift on a 4th unseen client by rotating all images by 90 degrees or changing the color saturation. Train FedPAT on the 3 source clients so that the prototype affinity topology is stored. Then run the model on the unseen shifted client using FedPAT (have the model make predictions), and compare accuracy and the magnitude of forgetting (how much accuracy drops on the source domain) against a baseline that adapts using only local feature statistics.
demo.closing: The demo must show that FedPAT keeps forgetting below 15 percent while improving shifted accuracy by at least 20 percent, because the global topology remembers the neighborhoods that hold across shifts, whereas local statistics crumble.
